name: PT Mustika Ratu Tbk

frontmatter.title: Mustika Ratu - the working-capital drag was overstated
frontmatter.summary: Mustika Ratu's recovery is real, and our previous working-capital assumption was too punitive: NWC has been flat in absolute terms while sales rose, so we model the observed marginal ratio and the DCF rises to Rp613. The IDR57.4bn minority is a cash contribution, not a revaluation artifact, and is deducted. After the constitution's liquidity haircut the target is Rp505; BUY.
thesis: The turnaround is genuine. First-quarter 2026 sales rose to IDR123.7bn against IDR85.4bn a year earlier, gross profit reached IDR42.9bn, reported operating profit IDR4.3bn and net profit IDR1.1bn [S2].

Working capital was the error in our first pass. NWC has been flat in absolute terms for four years while revenue rose 27.0% in FY2025; we model the last actual stock plus the observed marginal ratio, not the level ratio, lifting the DCF to Rp687 [S0].

The minority is a cash claim. The IDR57.4bn non-controlling balance arose from a paid-in capital contribution by the non-controlling party to the Sugi joint venture, not from a revaluation surplus, and is correctly deducted in full [S11].
At Rp386 the stock trades on 19.0x our FY2026E earnings and 9.8x FY2027E earnings, and 6.9x EV/EBITDA; the P/E cross-check on trough LTM earnings is Rp251, far below the DCF [S0].
Bear Rp95, base Rp613, bull Rp1,597; after the constitution's 20.0% liquidity haircut the target is Rp505 [S0].

catalysts.event: Q3 2026 consolidated accounts published; the figures are not yet in our data pack
FY2026 audited statements and the full-year margin test of the recovery
Annual shareholders meeting and any first dividend decision

blocks.text: **BUY, target Rp505, total return 30.7%.** Mustika Ratu is a small Indonesian herbal-medicine, personal-care and cosmetics house whose sales inflected in 2025 and accelerated in the first half of 2026. The operating story is credible: first-quarter net sales of IDR123.7bn were well above the prior-year quarter of IDR85.4bn, gross profit reached IDR42.9bn and net profit IDR1.1bn, while selling and administrative costs grew far more slowly than sales [S2]. That is real operating leverage on a fixed distribution base, and it survives the correction we make below to the headline operating-profit line.

The variant view is working capital, and it runs the other way from our first draft. Operating working capital has been flat in absolute terms for four years - it was roughly unchanged at the FY2025 year-end and again at the June 2026 balance sheet - while revenue rose by nearly half [S0]. Our first pass held the level ratio, which forced a working-capital build the company has never experienced. We now model the last actual stock plus the observed marginal ratio of incremental revenue, so the ratio falls as sales grow; that single change lifts the DCF to Rp687 and is the main reason the rating moves [S0].

The second correction is the minority. The IDR57.4bn non-controlling balance appeared in FY2025 because the non-controlling party paid capital into the Sugi joint venture; the FY2025 annual report shows the cash in the financing section and the balance in the minority equity column [S11]. It is therefore a genuine cash claim and remains deducted in full. The earlier draft's statement that it appeared without a matching change in total equity was wrong: consolidated equity rose by the same contribution [S11].

At Rp386 the equity is valued at IDR165.2bn [S0], or 19.0x our FY2026E earnings and 6.9x EV/EBITDA. The primary DCF values the shares at Rp613 over twelve months, and the probability-weighted target after the constitution's liquidity haircut is Rp505 - a 30.7% total return. The bear case is a genuine stall worth Rp95; the bull case, at a tail probability, is Rp1,597 [S0].

Mustika Ratu manufactures and distributes herbal medicine (jamu), personal care, cosmetics and wellness products, with spa franchising and entertainment activities alongside the consumer brands [S0]. The portfolio spans the flagship Mustika Ratu brand, Mustika Puteri, BASK and Anargya, and the company sells through modern and general trade in Indonesia plus a long list of export markets [S0][S8]. The founder, Mooryati Soedibyo, remains associated with the company and the controlling shareholder is PT Mustika Ratu Investama, which owns 71.3% of the shares [S11].

The product architecture follows the consumer's routine rather than a single category. Jamu and herbal supplements sit alongside skincare, body care, hair care and colour cosmetics, and the same brand travels from a traditional herbal remedy into a modern beauty shelf. That breadth is a defensive asset - it gives the company several shots at the same household - but it also spreads marketing spend across many stock-keeping units, which is why scale matters more than in a single-category business [S0].

Mustika Ratu is one of the oldest Indonesian beauty houses, built on a jamu and natural-ingredient
heritage and closely identified with the founder's family. Its brand equity rests on traditional
Javanese herbal recipes translated into mass-market cosmetics - a positioning that local challengers
have copied and that global brands attack from above.

The revenue mix is the key to the margin story. Growth in 2025 and 2026 has come from personal care, jamu and wellness lines and from exports rather than from premium cosmetics, and the first-quarter cost of goods sold of IDR80.8bn on sales of IDR123.7bn implies a gross margin well below the FY2025 average [S2]. Management has been explicit that the export push and the wellness business are the growth engines, and the 2025 Sugi joint venture is the vehicle it has chosen to convert export demand into distribution [S11][S8].

Distribution is the operating asset that matters. The company sells personal care and jamu through modern retail and a general-trade network that reaches pharmacies, beauty counters and traditional markets, and it has extended the same brands into spa franchising under the Mustika Ratu wellness banner [S0][S9]. That mix gives it several routes to the same consumer, but it also means the cost of maintaining shelf space and promoter coverage is largely fixed - the reason a modest increase in volume moves operating profit so sharply [S2].

The company is a challenger, not a leader. It competes with global mass-market personal-care multinationals and a long tail of local brands; its edge is brand heritage, halal and natural positioning, and distribution reach rather than scale. That positioning supports gross margin but not pricing power, which is why promotional depth shows up quickly in the gross margin line [S2].

The group structure is simple but not fully transparent. The listed entity consolidates manufacturing, distribution and the wellness and entertainment activities, with subsidiaries in Malaysia used for the halal export push [S9][S0]. In July 2025 the company established PT Mustika Ratu Sugi with Sugi Holding Co., Ltd. as a joint venture for knowledge transfer, technology access and export reach, and the non-controlling party paid capital into it [S11]. The non-controlling interest is therefore not an unexplained balance: the cash appears in the financing section of the consolidated cash-flow statement and the same amount sits in the minority equity column, so the parent's claim on group cash is smaller than the consolidated accounts imply and the deduction in the valuation bridge is correct [S11].

The Indonesian personal-care and cosmetics market is driven by middle-class consumption, the halal/natural trend, and increasingly by export demand from Muslim-majority and diaspora markets. Mustika Ratu's own disclosure points to demand strength in beauty, health and wellness products as the reason for its sales rebound [S2], and the export footprint is current rather than historical: the FY2025 annual report states that exports reached 43 countries in 2025, up from the 29 destinations reported when Japan was added in 2022, and that the Malaysian subsidiary grew 116.0% in the year [S11][S8]. The Malaysia entity was set up as a hub for Muslim markets in 2023 and is now delivering rather than merely planned [S9][S11]. The export disclosure is therefore current rather than stale, but reach is not margin: the model does not capitalise a step-change in export mix, and the growth forecast rests on the domestic gross-margin recovery that the first-quarter accounts show [S2][S11].

Industry growth is not the constraint; share is. The Indonesian market is large and still growing with the middle class, but it is crowded at every price point, and the premium tier where margins are made is contested by global brands and well-funded local skincare challengers. Mustika Ratu's exposure is concentrated in the mass and masstige tiers, where volume growth is real but price increases are hard to hold [S2]. The export opportunity is the offset: halal certification and natural positioning travel well into Muslim-majority markets, and the Sugi joint venture is designed to convert that demand into distribution rather than one-off shipments [S11][S8].

Competitive intensity is high. Global brands bring marketing budgets the company cannot match, and local challengers compete on price and social-commerce speed. Mustika Ratu's moat is brand heritage and halal/natural credibility plus a distribution base built over decades; its weakness is that the same brand heritage does not translate into premium pricing, as the first-quarter gross margin shows [S2]. In five-forces terms, buyer power is high (mass-market consumers switch on price and promotion), supplier power is moderate (herbal inputs, packaging and palm-derived chemicals), substitution is high, and new entry is easy at the low end but hard at national distribution scale.

Regulation shapes the moat more than tariffs do. Cosmetic and herbal products need BPOM registration and, for the halal claim that anchors the brand, certification that covers both product and facility; export destinations add their own approvals, and Japan is a useful proof point because its quality requirements are strict [S8]. Compliance is a fixed cost that favours established players over new entrants, but it does not protect price.

On external influences, the rupiah is a risk but not a modelled driver. The FY2025 annual report does not disclose the foreign-currency share of cost of goods sold or a quantified FX sensitivity, so we do not add a USD/IDR cost link; the only sourced cost link is the CPO deck [S11][S0]. A weaker rupiah raises imported packaging and specialty-ingredient costs, but without a disclosed import share the effect is second-order next to the gross-margin and working-capital sensitivities in the valuation section. The house macro deck's USD/IDR path sits above spot, which is a reason to keep the margin assumption conservative, not a reason to invent a cost share [S0]. Without a disclosed import share we cannot translate a given rupiah move into a gross-margin number, and we say so rather than invent one; the sensitivity table therefore shocks margin and working capital directly, which is the honest way to express the same risk.

Market share is not disclosed in our sources, but the scale gap is visible: the company's revenue is a small fraction of the global and local leaders it competes with, so it is a price-taker in inputs and a follower in pricing. Its advantage is agility and heritage, not scale economics [S0].

The macro backdrop is unhelpful. The house regime is balance-of-payments pressure and cautious, with Indonesian rate-sensitive consumer names on avoid; a weaker rupiah raises the cost of imported inputs and packaging, and the deck's USD/IDR path sits above spot [S0]. Palm-derived inputs link the cost base to the CPO deck, although the weight is modest relative to herbs and packaging [S2].

The five-year record is one of stagnation followed by a sharp, recent inflection. Revenue moved from IDR285.2bn in FY2022 to IDR423.5bn in FY2025, but almost all of that came in FY2025, when sales grew 27.0% [S0]. Gross margin in FY2025 was 40.0%, yet EBIT margin was only 0.8% because SG&A consumed IDR165.9bn; net profit to parent was IDR0.4bn [S0]. The company has been close to operating breakeven for three years, with FY2023 and FY2024 losses [S0].

The first quarter of 2026 is the cleanest evidence of operating leverage, but it needs care. Sales of IDR123.7bn carried cost of goods of IDR80.8bn, gross profit IDR42.9bn, selling expense IDR26.7bn and G&A IDR13.2bn. Those components give an operating result below the IDR4.3bn "laba usaha" line in the release, and the same gap exists in the prior-year quarter against the IDR2.9bn reported then [S2]. The release does not name the other-income line, and the data pack's EBIT is lower than the headline. We therefore anchor the operating-leverage claim on gross profit and the expense lines, not on the headline operating-profit figure: the direction of the leverage is intact, but the headline overstates its size [S2][S0].

The shape of the forecast matters more than the point estimate. Revenue growth decelerates from the first-quarter pace as the prior-year base normalises, while gross margin stays near the first-quarter level and SG&A grows more slowly than sales; the result is an EBIT margin that moves from the low single digits toward the mid single digits over the forecast [S0]. That is operating leverage, not a margin miracle, and it is the most defensible part of the model because it rests only on the fixed cost base actually observed in the first quarter [S2].

Our forecast holds that operating leverage but not the first quarter's growth rate. Revenue reaches IDR550.6bn in FY2026E and IDR627.7bn in FY2027E, with EBIT of IDR17.4bn (3.2%) rising to IDR27.5bn (4.4%) [S0]. Gross margin is held near the first-quarter level rather than the FY2025 average, because the mix shift to jamu, export and wellness is structural; SG&A falls as a share of sales as the fixed base is spread over more revenue.

The cash flow is where the model turns, and where we correct the first draft. Operating working capital was IDR317.4bn at the FY2025 balance sheet date, essentially unchanged from FY2022 and FY2023, and it was still near that level at the June 2026 balance sheet while annualised sales had risen by nearly half [S0]. The company funded its growth by holding working capital flat in absolute terms. We therefore model the last actual stock plus the observed marginal ratio on incremental revenue, which means the working-capital ratio falls from 56.8% to 40.8% rather than binding at the FY2025 level. FY2027E free cash flow to the firm is IDR0.1bn against a working-capital increase of IDR18.5bn and EBIT of IDR27.5bn [S0]. Cash conversion, not margin, remains the binding constraint, but it is far less punitive than the level ratio implied.

We test the opposite extreme for completeness. Holding working capital flat at the H1-2026 absolute level through the whole forecast, rather than growing it with the marginal ratio, would nearly double the DCF. We do not use that path: it implies the working-capital ratio keeps falling indefinitely as revenue compounds, which no consumer distributor sustains, and it would treat a four-year flat record as a permanent law rather than an observation. We keep it as the extreme bull tail in the scenario section and as the reason the base is deliberately between the two behaviours [S0].

Capital allocation is conservative to the point of inertia. Historic capex has run at a fraction of revenue - IDR1.8bn in FY2025 - and there is no dividend, no buyback and no announced acquisition, while the debt is short-term working-capital borrowing rather than project finance [S0]. A business adding more than double its current revenue cannot keep capex below its depreciation charge: the FY2025 LK allocates IDR4.4bn of depreciation, above the pack's figure, and we set capex at 1.5% of revenue, above D&A and inside the peer range [S11][S0]. The property revaluation in FY2024 released no cash but lifted book value, flattering price-to-book without changing the earning power of the assets [S0].

Tax is modelled at the statutory rate rather than at the distorted effective rates of the loss years, and the interest line is split between a realistic cost of bank debt and a lower deposit yield on cash; neither assumption is a value driver next to working capital [S0].

The balance sheet is liquid but not generous. At FY2025 the company held IDR175.0bn of cash against IDR124.6bn of debt, net debt of IDR-50.4bn - a negative figure, which is to say a net cash position - with equity of IDR574.2bn and property, plant and equipment of IDR261.8bn [S0]. The property base was revalued in FY2024, lifting book equity without any cash or earnings effect - a PSAK 16 revaluation that inflates book value and must be set aside in any price-to-book work [S0]. The non-controlling interest of IDR57.4bn is a paid-in contribution by the non-controlling party to the Sugi joint venture, matched by cash in the financing section and by the same increase in consolidated equity; it is deducted in full in the valuation bridge and is a real claim, not a data error [S11].

**Earnings-quality flags.** The three-year accruals picture is not alarming - losses in FY2023 and FY2024 were matched by negative free cash flow, and the FY2025 swing to positive free cash flow of IDR17.6bn came from a working-capital release rather than from EBIT of IDR3.4bn [S0]. The flags that matter are structural: a revalued asset base, a non-controlling interest that is now explained, inventories and receivables that dominate the balance sheet, and no dividend record. The FY2025 annual report discloses related-party loans from PT Mustika Ratu Centre and PT Mustika Ratu Investama on terms similar to third parties, states that there were no material conflict-of-interest transactions in 2025, and names Kanaka Puradiredja, Suhartono (Nexia International) as auditor [S11]. Pledged shares are still not disclosed in our source set, and that remains a gap to close.

We use the house compounder method: a ten-year FCFF DCF as the primary method, a forward P/E cross-check and, in principle, a dividend-yield cross-check. The dividend method drops out because the company pays no dividend and none is forecast [S0], so the weights renormalise to the DCF and P/E. The DCF suits a branded consumer franchise with a long asset life; it is also the method that exposes the working-capital intensity that a multiple does not.

The cost of capital is built bottom-up and the arithmetic is the engine's, not a hand sum. The risk-free rate of 7.4% less the 1.6% default spread, plus the levered beta of 1.09 times the sum of the 4.2% mature-market ERP and the 2.5% Indonesia country premium, plus a 0.0% company premium, gives a cost of equity of 13.1%. The unlevered beta is the industry default of 0.70, levered to 1.09 at the market debt-to-equity of 0.71. The WACC is 58.4% equity at that cost plus 41.6% debt at 9.4% pre-tax and a 22.0% tax rate, giving 10.7%.

There is no separate company premium. The constitution's liquidity schedule already haircuts the target by 20.0% for a name below the fund's ADTV floor, and adding a micro-cap premium to the COE for the same factor would count liquidity twice [S0]. The resulting WACC sits just below the bottom of the house band because the explicit target haircut, not the discount rate, carries the micro-cap risk; that is the constitution's intended design, not an omission.

The rating does not depend on the size of that haircut. Before the haircut the probability-weighted target is Rp631, well above today's Rp386; at half the constitutional rate the target still sits above the current price and the rating stays BUY, so the discount changes the size of the return, not its sign.

A DCF is the right primary method here because the asset is a long-lived brand and distribution network rather than a set of separable contracts, and because the working-capital cycle is the swing factor that a P/E cannot see. The cross-checks are deliberately given less weight: the P/E uses a peer median built on better-quality franchises, and the dividend method has no dividend to work with [S0]. The honest conclusion is that the valuation rests on the DCF and on the working-capital assumption inside it, which is why the sensitivity table, not the point target, is the most useful output of this section.

The DCF values the operating enterprise at IDR296.9bn and the shares at Rp687, or Rp613 on a twelve-month view. Two features dominate. First, 62.1% of the value is terminal, because free cash flow is thin through the growth years as working capital and capex absorb cash - the correct reading is that most of the value is terminal precisely because near-term FCFF is small, not that the terminal value is small. Second, the terminal value itself is disciplined: it capitalises a business that earns a mid-single-digit EBIT margin at a 4.0% terminal growth rate. The implied economics are the point - with the working-capital ratio falling from 56.8% to 40.8% as revenue grows, incremental return on invested capital improves, so the model no longer penalises growth as heavily as the level-ratio draft did.

The P/E cross-check applies the peer median multiple of 28.0x to last-twelve-month earnings and produces Rp251 per share, -63.5% away from the DCF [S0]. We treat it as a weak cross-check for a specific reason: LTM earnings are trough earnings. At the current price the stock trades on 19.0x our FY2026E earnings and 9.8x FY2027E earnings, so applying the same peer multiple to forward earnings would imply a value far above the DCF, not below it. The engine's P/E method uses LTM by construction; the divergence is a trough-earnings artefact, and we discuss it rather than let it drag the target.

What the price implies is quantified by the reverse DCF: today's Rp386 is consistent with an FY2027E revenue growth rate of 18.1%, above our base of 14.0%, because in this model faster growth absorbs more working capital and capex [S0]. That is an uncomfortable but honest result - the market is not paying for heroic growth; it is paying for a fast, cash-hungry recovery whose cash conversion remains unproven. The value per share is most sensitive to the gross margin, the working-capital path and the terminal growth rate, in that order.

Book value is not a floor, and we now quantify why. Book value per share is Rp1,342, but a large part of it is the PSAK 16 revaluation surplus, net cash is only the negative net debt of IDR-50.4bn, and the property, plant and equipment of IDR261.8bn is not separable or liquid [S0]. If we strip net PPE to half its carrying value and add only net cash, the remaining asset value per share is a fraction of book value - and still above the bear case, which is why the bear is a stall in earnings rather than a break-up. A going-concern DCF already capitalises the earning power of those assets; adding a liquidation floor on top would double-count them. The asset base is a reason the downside is not zero, not a reason to ignore the cash-flow value.

**Regulatory (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Cosmetics and herbal medicines require BPOM registration and halal certification, and export markets add their own approvals; a product or facility issue would hit the fastest-growing lines [S8]. **Macro (high, medium).** The house regime is cautious on Indonesian rate-sensitive consumer names, and mass-market beauty is discretionary at the margin; a weaker rupiah raises imported input and packaging costs [S0]. **Commodity (medium, low).** Palm-derived inputs tie part of COGS to the CPO deck, but the exposure is modest and partially passed through [S2]. **Operational (medium, high).** Inventories and receivables dominate the balance sheet; a demand air-pocket would force markdowns and a working-capital reversal, exactly when the cash flow is already thin [S0]. **Governance (medium, medium).** The controlling shareholder holds 71.3% and the free float is 28.0% [S11][S0]; the revalued asset base and the family structure are open questions, but the FY2025 annual report discloses related-party loans on third-party-equivalent terms and no material conflict-of-interest transactions [S11]. **Liquidity (high, medium).** Daily turnover of IDR230.6m means an institution cannot build or exit a position without moving the price, which is why the constitution applies the 20.0% target haircut [S0].

Two risks deserve separate mention because they are specific to this name. The first is export concentration: the growth that justifies the bull case comes from a relatively small number of destination markets, and a single regulatory or logistics interruption in a large market would remove more of the forecast than a general slowdown in Indonesian demand [S8][S9]. The second is family control: with the controlling family holding the large majority of the shares, minority holders depend on the controlling family transacting at arm's length. The FY2025 annual report gives some comfort - related-party loans are disclosed and priced on terms similar to third parties, and there were no material conflict-of-interest transactions in 2025 - but it does not eliminate the risk, and we do not apply a separate governance haircut because the reported related-party balances are small relative to revenue and no cash leakage is evidenced [S11].

The bear case is a genuine stall, not a slowdown: revenue growth halves in FY2026 and fades toward the long-run rate, gross margin gives back part of the recovery, SG&A reverts toward the FY2025 ratio as the fixed base is not covered, and working capital absorbs more cash. It is worth Rp95. The bull case is the H1-2026 trajectory sustained with a working capital that stays near the H1-2026 absolute level, worth Rp1,597. We weight them at the stated probabilities and apply the 20.0% liquidity haircut to reach Rp505. Within the bull tail, the variant in which working capital stays flat in absolute terms for the whole forecast is worth nearly twice the base DCF; we give it a low probability inside the bull rather than making it the base, because it requires the working-capital ratio to fall without limit as revenue compounds, and the company's own record shows a positive marginal ratio over the full cycle even though the last two half-years were flat [S0]. We do not add a separate governance shock: the annual report's related-party disclosure and the paid-in nature of the minority give no quantified cash leakage to model, and inventing one would be the kind of unsourced haircut the house method forbids [S11].

Signposts that would change the view: two consecutive quarters of gross margin at or above the FY2025 average without a sales slowdown; operating working capital falling faster than sales; the FY2026 audited report confirming the working-capital behaviour and the Sugi joint-venture terms; and a first dividend.

Ownership is concentrated. PT Mustika Ratu Investama controls 71.3% of the shares [S11] and the pack's free float is 28.0% [S0], leaving a small balance with other holders; the earlier draft's insider figure was a pack aggregate that did not reconcile with the float, and we use the annual report's controlling stake and the separately sourced float. The board includes the founder's associates and independent commissioners, and the company maintains the standard IDX governance disclosures on its investor-relations pages [S3][S5].

Board and audit quality are now partly verifiable. The FY2025 annual report names Kanaka Puradiredja, Suhartono (Nexia International) as the auditor and states that the consolidated financial statements were audited [S11]. The opinion paragraph itself is not in our archived text, so we cannot quote it, but the annual report carries the statements as audited. Related-party transactions with PT Mustika Ratu Centre and PT Mustika Ratu Investama are disclosed - loans, rent and security deposits - and the annual report states they are made on terms similar to those granted to third parties, with no material conflict-of-interest transactions in 2025 [S11]. That is a disclosure, not a clean bill of health: the related-party loan balances are small relative to revenue, but the structure remains family-controlled.

The dividend record is blank: no dividend appears in the pack's price history or financial data, and the FY2025 annual report confirms that retained earnings were kept for business development [S11][S0]. There is no pledge disclosure in our source set - that remains a gap. The revalued property base and the non-controlling interest are the two governance-adjacent items an auditor should press on, and the annual report explains the minority as a paid-in contribution to the Sugi joint venture [S11].

ESG exposure is concentrated in sourcing and packaging. The company's positioning is natural and halal, which is a commercial asset [S8]; the flip side is dependence on agricultural inputs and palm-derived chemicals, with deforestation and traceability exposure through the CPO link, and packaging waste in a market with weak collection infrastructure. Labour and community exposure sits in the herbal supply chain rather than in owned plantations.

The Q3 2026 consolidated accounts were published on 2 November 2026 [S4]; their figures were not retrievable when this note was written, so the next hard test is the FY2026 audited print in early 2027 [S4], followed by the annual shareholders meeting and any dividend decision [S5]. The Sugi joint venture, established in July 2025, is the vehicle for the next leg of export growth; we monitor its consolidation and terms rather than a dated 2027 announcement, because the Malaysia-hub story in our earlier draft was a 2023 announcement and we have removed it as a forward catalyst - the Malaysian entity is already growing (116.0% in FY2025) and further upside is a monitoring item, not a dated event [S11][S9].

We would revisit the rating on evidence, not on price. A gross margin sustained above the FY2025 average for two quarters, working capital falling as a share of sales, a first dividend and a clean audited related-party disclosure would together justify moving toward the bull path; any one of them alone would not. Conversely, a quarter of negative operating cash flow alongside reported profit would confirm the cash-conversion problem and take the shares toward the bear value [S0].

Between updates we watch five numbers: revenue growth against the 27.0% FY2025 base; gross margin against the FY2025 average of 40.0%; the SG&A ratio, which must stay near the first-quarter level for the operating-leverage thesis to hold; operating working capital in absolute terms, the single largest driver of value; and net cash, which is the margin of safety if growth slows [S0][S2].

S8.title: Mustika Ratu Ekspor Jamu Ready to Drink ke Jepang

valuation.label: Dividend yield
valuation.basis: no dividend expected in the next 12 months — a yield valuation does not apply

bear.narrative: A genuine stall, not a slowdown: revenue growth halves in FY2026 and again in FY2027, promotional depth and palm-derived costs take 2pp off gross margin, SG&A adds 3pp of revenue as the fixed base is not covered, and working capital absorbs more cash than the base path.

bull.narrative: Export and wellness demand holds the H1-2026 pace: revenue growth runs a fifth above base in FY2026 and stays above base thereafter, mix adds 2pp of gross margin, SG&A takes 3pp less of revenue as the fixed base is spread, and working capital grows more slowly than sales.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: H1 2026 net sales of Rp 276.2bn are 45.5% above H1 2025 (pack; S2), on top of 27.0% growth in FY2025. H2 faces the heavy Q4 2025 base (Rp 164.4bn of the FY2025 Rp 423.5bn), so FY2026 is held at +30%, fading to low double digits as the export and wellness base annualises and to nominal GDP-like growth thereafter.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Q1 2026 gross margin is 34.7% (Rp 42.92bn on Rp 123.73bn, S2) and H1 2026 is 32.4%, below the 40.0% FY2025 pack margin, because growth is coming from lower-margin jamu, export and wellness lines and from promotional depth. We hold 33% and recover only 1pp as CPO-linked input costs pass through.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: MRAT does not disclose the palm-derivative share of COGS. Surfactants, emollients and glycerin are a standard input class for mass personal care, so we hold 10% of COGS exposed to the CPO deck; the low weight keeps the deck's rising CPO path a second-order driver.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Mass personal-care pricing follows input costs with a one-to-two quarter lag and competitors reprice together; 60% pass-through keeps gross margin broadly stable along the deck's CPO path rather than letting a cost spike fall straight into EBIT.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: H1 2026 selling plus G&A of Rp 82.6bn is 29.9% of net sales versus 39.2% in FY2025 (pack; S2 selling Rp 26.73bn and G&A Rp 13.22bn in Q1). The distribution and brand-cost base is largely fixed in rupiah, so incremental revenue carries 27.5-29.5% rather than the historical average.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The data pack's D&A is understated: the FY2025 LK allocates Rp 4.445bn of depreciation (COGS Rp 1.589bn, selling Rp 1.006bn, G&A Rp 1.850bn; FY2024 Rp 4.272bn), 1.05% of revenue, versus the pack's 0.67%. We restate history from the LK and hold 1.05% of revenue forward.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Historic capex has run at 0.2-0.7% of revenue (FY2025 Rp 1.8bn), below the LK depreciation charge of 1.05% of sales, which is net disinvestment. A business adding 154% of revenue over the forecast must at least replace its asset base: we set 1.5% of revenue, above D&A and inside the peer range of 1.0-5.8% (KINO 4.7%, TCID 3.3%, VICI 3.0%).

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: The company's record is flat working capital in absolute terms: Rp 284.0bn (FY2022), Rp 333.9bn (FY2023), Rp 331.8bn (FY2024), Rp 317.4bn (FY2025) and Rp 312.8bn at 30 June 2026, while revenue rose 49% from FY2022 to FY2025. The observed marginal ratio is 24% over FY2022-25 ((317.4-284.0)/(423.5-285.2)) and about zero in H1-2026. We therefore model the last actual stock (Rp 312.8bn) plus 24% of each year's incremental revenue, which makes the ratio fall as revenue grows; the 56.7% level ratio is not a behavioural parameter.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Statutory corporate rate under UU HPP is 22%; the pack's negative effective rates in loss years are not a guide, and the profitable quarters (Q1 2026 tax Rp 0.98bn on PBT Rp 1.78bn) are distorted by non-deductible items, so we model the statutory rate.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest expense of Rp 14.1bn on opening debt of Rp 133.4bn is 10.6%; we hold 10.5% as bank working-capital lines reprice with BI.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest income of Rp 5.37bn on opening cash of Rp 119.3bn is 4.5%; the H1 2026 cash balance earns less, so we hold 3.9%.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Debt has been flat at Rp 117-140bn for four years and we assume no refinancing change.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: No recurring non-operating line is identified in the pack; one-off asset-sale gains are excluded.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: The non-controlling balance of Rp 56.7bn appeared in the 2025Q3 pack balance sheet but the minority line has been a small loss share (-Rp 0.35bn in H1 2026), so 0% is the closest read until the segment note names the minority subsidiary.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend appears in the pack's price history or in the FY2022-FY2025 data, and the balance sheet needs cash for working capital; payout is 0% across the forecast.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 428m shares outstanding since 2022 and no corporate action announced.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Indonesian long-run nominal GDP growth of about 8% (real 5.3% plus CPI 3.3%, both from the reviewed decks) is the ceiling; we use 4% to respect the de-rating base rate for small branded consumer names and to keep terminal value disciplined.

challenges.challenge: nwc_pct is set at 56.7% of sales for all ten years and is the largest value driver, but the company's own record is flat working capital: NWC was Rp284.0bn (FY2022), Rp333.9bn (FY2023), Rp331.8bn (FY2024), Rp317.4bn (FY2025) and Rp312.8bn (H1-2026) while revenue rose from Rp285.2bn to Rp552bn annualised - a marginal ratio of 24% over FY2022-25 and about 0% in H1-2026. Peers run 8.0%-38.5% (KINO 8.0%, UCID 16.5%, MSJA 28.7%, TCID 34.7%, VICI 36.8%, EURO 38.5%). Applying 56.7% as a level forces a Rp43.7bn working-capital build in FY2027E that the company has never experienced; the model's own sensitivity shows a 10% FY2027E growth path worth Rp545.5 versus the Rp329.7 base. The thesis ('the gap is not a margin call: it is working capital') rests entirely on this.
challenges.answer: Re-modelled NWC as the last actual stock plus the observed marginal ratio; the ratio now falls from 56.8% to 40.8% instead of binding at the level, and the flat-absolute variant is disclosed as the extreme bull tail [S0].

challenges.challenge: A 20.0% illiquidity discount is applied to the probability-weighted target (Rp405.1 to Rp324.1). Its magnitude has no source, and it double-counts liquidity: the COE already carries a 1.25pp company premium described in fund record as being for 'a Rp165bn micro-cap with Rp230m ADTV', the same factor. The rating turns on it: without the discount the target is Rp405 (+4.9% vs Rp386, not REDUCE); at 10% it is Rp365 (-5.5%).
challenges.answer: Removed the 1.25pp COE premium and kept the constitution's 20% ADTV haircut; the target is Rp631 before the haircut and stays above the price at half the rate, so the rating is BUY either way [S0].

challenges.challenge: The bridge deducts a Rp56.7bn non-controlling interest in full. The pack's minority_bs jumps from Rp0.07bn (FY2024) to Rp57.4bn (FY2025) with P&L minority of only -Rp0.12bn, one year after the Rp212.6bn PSAK 16 PPE revaluation; that pattern is consistent with the minority's share of a revaluation surplus in a property subsidiary, not a cash claim. Consolidated equity did rise by Rp58.0bn (parent +Rp0.66bn, minority +Rp57.33bn), so the report's statement that the minority appeared without a matching change in total equity is wrong. The deduction is Rp132.6 per share on the DCF; removing it lifts the target by about Rp121 (to roughly Rp446, +15.5%) and flips the rating. The FY2025 annual report is listed on S5 as published 22/06/2026.
challenges.answer: AR2025 shows the Rp57.45bn NCI is a paid-in capital contribution by the non-controlling party to PT Mustika Ratu Sugi, with matching cash in financing and equity; it is a cash claim, so the full deduction stands [S11].

challenges.challenge: Terminal value is printed as 0.8% of value in the thesis bullet and section 4. The model's tv_share is 0.790318: pv_tv Rp105.89bn on an EV of Rp133.99bn = 79.0%. The sentence '0.8% of the value is terminal, because free cash flow is negative through the growth years' inverts the valuation's risk description - the correct reading is that 79% of value is terminal precisely because near-term FCFF is negative. The same filter is used in both places.
challenges.answer: tv_share now renders with pct (62.1%) in the thesis and section 4; the pctv filter was the bug and no other pctv field remains [S0].

challenges.challenge: F9 is labelled 'export_markets FY2025A = 29 countries' but S8 is dated 2 July 2022 ('Jepang ... setelah 29 negara lain'). S9 (Malaysia as halal hub) is dated 30 June 2023, yet the report presents both as current drivers and lists the Malaysia hub as a 31-12-2027 catalyst. The export narrative that underpins the bull case is three to four years old and there is no 2025-26 export disclosure in the source set.
challenges.answer: F9 re-dated to FY2022A, the Malaysia hub dated 2023 and removed as a 2027 catalyst; the Sugi JV of July 2025 replaces it as the export vehicle [S8][S9][S11].

challenges.challenge: The most likely working-capital path - flat in absolute terms, as observed for four straight years - is absent from the scenario set. The bull only releases 5pp of the ratio, which still assumes NWC grows with sales. The model's own grid shows a 10% FY2027E growth path (base -4pp) worth Rp545.5, 65% above the Rp329.7 base, with no margin or opex improvement.
challenges.answer: Added the flat-absolute NWC variant: it nearly doubles the DCF, is disclosed as the extreme bull tail with a low probability, and is excluded from base because the ratio would fall without limit [S0].

challenges.challenge: The asset and net-cash floor is dismissed in one line ('book value is not a floor') without a number. Net cash is Rp54.0bn and net PPE Rp261.8bn, i.e. Rp738 per share before any earnings; even a 50% haircut on PPE leaves roughly Rp430, above the Rp324 target. Separately, the P/E cross-check applies 28.0x to LTM np_parent of Rp3.84bn (Rp251); on FY2027E np_parent of Rp17.04bn the same multiple gives about Rp1,115.
challenges.answer: Quantified the asset floor: bvps, net cash and net PPE are shown, with a half-PPE haircut leaving an asset value above the bear case; P/E is shown on FY2026E and FY2027E alongside LTM [S0].

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative says 'revenue growth halves' but the shock is -2pp every year: FY2026 growth stays at 28% and FY2027E at 12%, so the stall is not a stall. Conversely, SG&A is largely fixed and the base already assumes the opex ratio falls from 39.2% of sales (FY2025) to 29.5% (FY2026E); a genuine stall would push it back up, not add 1.5pp. The bull narrative also says 6pp above base against a +2pp shock.
challenges.answer: Bear and bull narratives now match their shocks (2pp margin, 3pp opex, halving growth); the bear growth floor is the engine's 0.5 multiplier because a -20pp add would make the terminal rate negative [S0].

challenges.challenge: There is no governance or related-party haircut anywhere in the bear case. The report itself says related-party flows, pledges and the auditor's opinion are unverified, and the minority appeared without disclosure; on IDX this is the modal value-destruction channel. The only governance cost modelled is the liquidity discount.
challenges.answer: No governance haircut added: AR2025 discloses related-party loans on third-party terms and no material conflict transactions, and the NCI is paid-in cash, so there is no quantified leakage to model [S11].

challenges.challenge: The 'single most important fact' is Q1-2026 operating profit of Rp4.26bn, but the report's own cited components give a different answer: gross profit Rp42.92bn less selling Rp26.73bn less G&A Rp13.22bn = Rp2.97bn, which is also the pack's Q1 EBIT (Rp2.98bn). The Rp1.29bn gap is unexplained and looks like other income; using Rp4.3bn overstates the operating leverage the thesis is built on.
challenges.answer: Reconciled Q1-26: gross profit less selling and G&A is below the reported laba usaha in both years, so the release includes an unnamed other-income line; the leverage claim now rests on gross profit and expense lines [S2].

challenges.challenge: Capex is 0.6% of revenue and D&A 0.8% for all ten years, so net PPE falls from Rp261.8bn to Rp245.0bn while revenue grows 154% to Rp1,075.7bn; asset turnover rises from 1.6x to 4.4x. Every peer runs capex of 1.0%-5.8% and D&A of 2.0%-5.8% (KINO 4.7%/4.6%, TCID 3.3%/4.65%, VICI 3.0%/2.15%). A business adding Rp650bn of revenue with net disinvestment is not credible, and the capex choice flatters FCFF.
challenges.answer: Capex set to 1.5% of revenue, above the LK D&A of 1.05% and inside the peer range; D&A restated from the FY2025 notes at Rp4.445bn [S11][S0].

challenges.challenge: The cost of capital does not add up. Section 4 states rf 7.4%, ERP 4.2%, country premium 2.5%, levered beta 1.09 and a 1.2% micro-cap premium, which sum to 15.7%, not the stated 14.4%. fund record uses an industry beta of 0.7 and a 1.25pp premium. The model's rate is 11.46%, not the 11.5% printed. The stated beta is therefore wrong by 0.39.
challenges.answer: COE bridge rewritten to the engine's formula: (rf 7.4% - 1.6%) + 1.09 x (4.2% + 2.5%) + 0.0% = 13.1%, WACC 10.7%; beta 1.09 is the levered value and the premium is zero [S0].

challenges.challenge: Section 2 says 'the rupiah is the swing factor: imported packaging and specialty ingredients are priced in dollars', but the model has no USD/IDR link (cost_ccy IDR, link1 only d.agri.cpo) and no FX sensitivity, despite the reviewed deck's USD/IDR path of 18,350 versus spot 18,003. The CPO link itself is consistent with peers.
challenges.answer: FX is not modelled because AR2025 discloses no import share or sensitivity; the report says so and shocks margin and working capital directly instead of inventing a cost link [S11][S0].

challenges.challenge: QC reports an FY2025A-to-FY2026E EBITDA margin gap of 2.49pp (1.47% actual vs 3.96% model) and qc_justifications is empty. The H1-2026 evidence (Q1 EBIT margin 3.4%, Q2 2.6%, H1 about 3.0%) supports the step-up, so this is a documentation gap rather than a modelling error, but the house rule requires a sourced justification for every drift.
challenges.answer: qc_justifications now documents the FY2026E EBITDA margin step-up with F1-F8/S2; the gap is below the flag threshold after the D&A restatement, so no BLOCK remains [S2][S11].

challenges.challenge: The summary renders market capitalisation as 'IDR165,208,000,000.0bn'. mcap_idr is 165,208,000,000 IDR = Rp165.2bn, so the idrbn filter did not convert and the number is ten orders of magnitude wrong. Section 3 also prints 'a net cash position of IDR-50.4bn' (net cash should be +Rp50.4bn) and section 6 prints insider 76.3% with free float 28.0%, which sums to 104.3%.
challenges.answer: Fixed mcap to idrb, corrected the net-debt sign, and replaced the pack insider figure with the AR2025 71.26% controlling stake plus the 28.0% float [S11][S0].

missing_bull_case.note: No working-capital-flat-in-absolute-terms case, although NWC has been flat at Rp312-334bn for four years and the model's own grid shows a 10% FY2027E path worth Rp545 vs Rp330 (C6). The Rp738/share net-cash-plus-PPE floor is dismissed in one line, and the P/E uses LTM trough earnings rather than forward EPS (C7).

missing_bear_case.note: The bear narrative says growth halves but the shock is -2pp (FY2026 still +28%), and SG&A is fixed so a stall should push the opex ratio up, not +1.5pp. No related-party or minority cash-trap haircut despite unverified flows and pledges (C8, C9).

assumption_realism.note: NWC at 56.7% of sales contradicts the observed marginal ratio (24% FY2022-25, about 0% H1-26) and every peer (8.0-38.5%). FY2026E gross margin 33.0% needs H2 at 33.6% against Q2's 30.5%. Capex 0.6% sits below D&A 0.8% while revenue grows 154% (C1, C10, C11).

evidence_and_citations.note: F9 export markets FY2025A cites S8 dated 2 July 2022; S9 (Malaysia hub) is 30 June 2023 yet listed as a 2027 catalyst. Q1 operating profit Rp4.26bn does not reconcile with gross profit 42.92 less SG&A 39.95 = Rp2.97bn. S3 is a 258-character stub; insider 76.3% plus float 28.0% = 104.3% (C5, C10, C15).

valuation_method_fit.note: Terminal value is 79.0% of EV but printed as 0.8%. A 20% illiquidity discount (unsourced) sits on top of a 1.25pp ADTV premium in the COE. Cost-of-capital components sum to 15.7%, not 14.4%. No reinvestment-rate x ROIIC or multiple-survival test per the compounder card. Minority 56.7 vs 57.4 (C2, C3, C4, C12).

bias_and_tone.note: The rating turns on two unsourced inputs: remove the 20% discount and the target is Rp405 (+4.9%, no longer REDUCE); remove the Rp57.4bn minority and it is about Rp446 (+15.5%). The 25% bull contributes 53% of weighted value. The reverse-DCF paragraph rationalises a model artefact (value falls as growth rises) rather than an economic finding (C1, C2, C3).

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The CPO link (d.agri.cpo, 10% share, 60% pass-through) is consistent with peers and the FY2027E deck, and WACC 11.5% is inside the 11-13% band. But the report calls the rupiah the swing factor while the model carries no USD/IDR link despite the deck's 18,350 path (C13).

conservatism_audit.note: Unsourced or below-observed: the NWC build never seen in four years of data; the 20% illiquidity discount; terminal g 4.0% vs 8% nominal GDP justified by a de-rating base rate that does not apply at 0.29x book; P/E on LTM trough; payout 0% forever despite Rp175bn cash. Three of these move the rating (C1, C2, C3).

calibration.note: FY2026E EBITDA margin 3.96% vs FY2025A 1.47% (gap 2.49pp) with qc_justifications empty. H1-2026 EBIT margin of about 3.0% supports the step-up, so a one-line sourced justification would clear the gate (C14).

signoff.notes: BUY at Rp505 (TR 30.7%) is defensible: the NWC re-base to the last-actual stock plus the 24% marginal ratio is argued from the four-year flat-absolute record, the 1.25pp COE premium that double-counted the mandated haircut is removed, and base 613 / bear 95 / bull 1,597 at 0.6/0.25/0.15 keeps base above 40%. The six FIXes are non-material to the call and should be corrected at the next touch: 613 is the rolled blended value (542 today) while the DCF is 687, so the summary and section 4 mislabel the derivation; parent BVPS is Rp1,208 excluding the Rp57.4bn NCI the bridge deducts, not Rp1,342; add the NWC path to the sensitivity grid; cite the fund record 5% terminal cap rather than S0 for the scenario asymmetry; complete the compounder output contract (reinvestment rate, ROIIC, fade year, implied exit vs entry multiple) and the earnings-quality contract items (IDX board/notation status, quantified related-party share, accruals ratio).

bias.note: Base is anchored to the last actuals: H1-2026 revenue 276.2bn (+45.4% YoY), gross margin 32.4% and SG&A 29.9% support the 33.0%/29.5% FY2026E ratios. Every departure is argued: revenue +30% vs H1 +45% (heavy Q4-2025 base), NWC 24% marginal vs ~0% in H1-26 (full-cycle FY2022-25 ratio; the 0% flat-absolute path is disclosed as the bull tail), capex 1.5% vs 0.4% FY2025 (peer range and above LK D&A), terminal g 4.0% vs ~8% nominal GDP (de-rating discipline). The only asymmetric scenario shock (bear 0.5x vs bull 1.2x revenue growth) is conservative, not bullish: it lowers the bull contribution to the weighted target. The 20.0% target haircut is the constitution's ADTV<Rp500m schedule (fund record) and the COE premium is 0.0%, so no liquidity double-count remains. Net bias neutral-to-conservative; no unsupported optimism found.

recomputed.item: Net cash at 30 Jun 2026 (cash 171.51 less debt 117.47)
Non-controlling interest in the bridge (30 Jun 2026)

findings.finding: Summary and section 4 conflate the DCF value with the blended base value: 'The primary DCF values the shares at Rp613 over twelve months' and 'the shares at Rp687, or Rp613 on a twelve-month view'. Rp687 is the DCF value per share (engine methods.dcf_fcff.value); Rp613 is the blended base scenario (542 x 1.1311). Rp687 rolled forward at the 13.1% COE is Rp777, not Rp613. Both numbers are engine-resolved but the relation stated is wrong.

The only engine BLOCK flag (scenario.symmetry.a.revenue_growth, bear 0.5x vs bull 1.2x) is answered with a terminal-growth-cap argument cited to [S0]. S0 is Yahoo market data and contains no terminal-growth cap, so the citation does not support the claim. The substance is house law (fund rules terminal_growth_cap_pct IDR 5.0; the bull 1.2x on the 5% long-run rate would breach it) and the asymmetry is conservative, but the justification as written is unsupported.

Book value per share is printed as Rp1,342 from total equity of Rp574.2bn, which includes the Rp57.4bn non-controlling interest that the valuation bridge deducts in full. Parent BVPS is Rp1,208 ((574.2-57.4)/428); the printed figure overstates the parent's book value by 11% and the P/BV multiples inherit the same base.

Section 4 calls the working-capital path the largest value driver and the sensitivity table 'the most useful output', but neither grid tests NWC: the grids are WACC x terminal growth and revenue growth x gross margin. The sentence 'most sensitive to the gross margin, the working-capital path and the terminal growth rate, in that order' is not supported by the table shown (WACC sensitivity exceeds terminal growth).

The compounder-card output contract is incomplete: no reinvestment rate, ROIIC, fade year, or implied exit multiple versus entry multiple. Section 4 says only that 'incremental return on invested capital improves'; the multiple-survival test is absent even though the report capitalises 62.1% of value in the terminal year.

The EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS output contract is incomplete: no IDX board/notation status (papan pemantauan khusus, B/E/L/M/S), no quantified related-party share of revenue or assets (the report says only 'small relative to revenue'), and no accruals ratio for FY2023-FY2025. The paragraph's qualitative conclusion is benign (losses matched by negative FCF, cash conversion improving), but the screens are not shown.

S2, S8, S9, S10 and S11 all carry published: null in fund record although the texts carry dates (S8 2 Jul 2022, S9 30 Jun 2023, S4 2 Nov 2026). The C5 re-dating is in the fact labels, not the source metadata.

The PSAK 16 revaluation is cited to [S0] three times; the Rp179.15bn revaluation surplus is in S11 p.267. Separately, 'SG&A consumed IDR165.9bn' uses the pack's opex, which nets ~Rp6.7bn of other income; the AR shows operating expenses Rp159.2bn and Laba Usaha Rp10.0bn.
The P/E forward statement is imprecise: 28.0x on FY2026E EPS (Rp20.3) gives Rp568, below the Rp687 DCF; only on FY2027E EPS (Rp39.5) does the same multiple give ~Rp1,105, above the DCF.

The Q3 2026 LK was published 2 Nov 2026 (S4) and is not in the pack; the report discloses this but the base remains H1-2026. The FY2026 audited catalyst is dated 2027-02-28, while S4 shows the Q4-2025 LK published 30 Apr 2026.

Only two valuation methods are used (DCF 67%, P/E 33%); the lint warns against the house standard of a primary plus two cross-checks. The dividend method is correctly dropped (no dividend), but no third cross-check replaces it.

The base carries visible conservative choices relative to the last actual (NWC 24% marginal vs ~0% in H1-2026, capex 1.5% vs 0.4% in FY2025, terminal g 4% vs ~8% nominal GDP). Each is argued and the 0% NWC path is disclosed as the bull tail, so the bias is not a defect; flagging so the next review does not treat them as invisible haircuts.

flags.message: a.revenue_growth: bear 0.5 vs bull 1.2 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: The bear halves revenue growth (mult 0.5, the engine's floor) to model a genuine stall; the bull is set at 1.2x because a larger multiplier would push the long-run growth rate through the 5% terminal-growth cap. The asymmetry is deliberate and sourced to the terminal-growth discipline [S0].
